result.question: Authentication stack for a 2026 self-hosted, multi-tenant B2B SaaS built on Next.js App Router (v15+) + TypeScript + Postgres, optimized for lean self-hosted VPS ops, data ownership, and scale-readiness. Compare the leading self-hostable auth libraries — Auth.js / NextAuth v5 (beta status?), Better Auth, Lucia (is it deprecated/EOL?), and any strong alternatives — for: (a) built-in organizations/teams + RBAC support, (b) session model options (database-backed revocable sessions vs stateless JWT) and revocation/"log out all devices", (c) 2FA/MFA — TOTP + recovery codes and WebAuthn/passkeys support, (d) email invitations + password reset flows with anti-user-enumeration, (e) working inside an INSTALLED PWA (httpOnly secure cookies, service worker, offline, and tying a Web Push subscription to the authenticated device/session), (f) production maturity, maintenance health, and security track record as of 2026. Also cover current security best practices for each of those areas and any notable CVEs/advisories. Conclude with a concrete recommendation (library + session model + 2FA approach) for this exact stack, plus a fallback if the primary choice is immature.
result.summary: For a 2026 self-hosted, multi-tenant B2B SaaS on Next.js App Router (v15+) + TypeScript + Postgres, Better Auth is the clear primary recommendation and the other two contenders are effectively out: Lucia is EOL (v3 deprecated by March 2025, now a "build auth from scratch" learning resource, npm package flagged deprecated), and Auth.js/NextAuth is in security-only maintenance under the Better Auth team, with passkeys still experimental on a perpetually-beta v5 — and its own maintainers now steer new projects to Better Auth. Better Auth is the only option with first-party multi-tenant organizations/teams + RBAC (owner/admin/member), database-backed revocable sessions with true "log out all devices," TOTP + single-use recovery codes, SimpleWebAuthn-based passkeys, and built-in anti-user-enumeration on sign-up. Recommended configuration: Better Auth with database-backed (revocable) sessions, TOTP + recovery codes as baseline MFA and passkeys as step-up/passwordless, pinned to current patched releases with revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset enabled and the session.cookieCache 2FA-bypass class of bug avoided. The main caveat is a security-maturity signal (31 advisories, 21 in 2026, including a critical premature-cookie-cache 2FA bypass and a high-severity org-invitation flaw that hit exactly the org + invitation features this stack uses), so version-pin and track the advisory feed; the fallback is Auth.js v5 with a Postgres adapter to gain revocable DB sessions, accepting no built-in orgs/RBAC and experimental passkeys. Note one hard web-platform constraint for the installed-PWA requirement: a service worker cannot read httpOnly cookies, so auth-state visibility, offline UX, and Web-Push-to-session binding must be designed around server endpoints, and the popular "two-cookie split" mitigation was NOT supported by the cited spec discussion.

findings.claim: Better Auth is the only one of the three with a first-party multi-tenant Organization plugin: organizations with optional teams, three default RBAC roles (owner/admin/member) with distinct permission scopes, and complete email-invitation flows (invite/accept/reject/cancel, 48h default expiry) requiring a developer-supplied sendInvitationEmail. [dimension a]
findings.evidence: Primary docs, the GitHub main-branch source MDX, and multi-source search all confirm the built-in Organization plugin ships owner (full control), admin (full control except delete-org/change-owner), and member (read-only) roles, with permissions across organization/member/invitation resources; teams are optional via teams.enabled:true on server+client (GitHub #6772 confirms owner/admin/member are the immutable defaults in 2026). Invitation functions map to inviteMember/acceptInvitation/rejectInvitation/cancelInvitation; invitationExpiresIn defaults to 48h and is configurable; sendInvitationEmail is developer-supplied and required for delivery. No comparable first-party orgs/teams/RBAC layer for Auth.js or Lucia surfaced in the verified claim set (would be custom-built).

findings.claim: Better Auth defaults to database-backed, server-revocable cookie sessions (with an optional stateless no-DB mode using signed/encrypted cookies) and ships built-in 'log out all devices' via revokeSession, revokeOtherSessions, and revokeSessions. [dimension b]
findings.evidence: Official session-management docs document a Session table, DB storage, and all three revocation APIs with the exact claimed semantics (revokeSession ends one; revokeOtherSessions ends all but current; revokeSessions ends all). A dedicated 'Stateless Session Management' section (shipped in Better Auth 1.4, ~Nov 2025) stores session data in a signed/encrypted cookie with no DB query, giving an explicit choice between revocable DB sessions and JWT-like stateless sessions; docs acknowledge stateless sessions can only be invalidated via versioning + redeploy. Corroborated by two independent doc mirrors and the 1.4 release notes. DB-backed default is what makes true server-side revocation work for this stack.

findings.claim: Auth.js/NextAuth defaults to stateless JWT sessions that cannot be revoked before their encoded expiry (sign-out only deletes the cookie; a JWT saved elsewhere stays valid); configuring a database adapter switches it to server-revocable DB sessions that enable 'sign out everywhere' and concurrent-login limits. [dimension b]
findings.evidence: authjs.dev/concepts/session-strategies states JWT is the default 'unless a database provider is configured,' that a JWT the user saved elsewhere 'will be valid...until it expires,' and that DB sessions 'can be at any time modified server-side' to implement 'sign out everywhere' or 'limiting concurrent logins.' The NextAuth options docs independently confirm default='jwt' but 'database' when an adapter is used. True server-side revocation is therefore NOT built in for the JWT strategy (requires a self-implemented blocklist). Consistent across NextAuth v4 and Auth.js v5 as of 2026; one nuance is that Credentials providers force JWT even with an adapter.

findings.claim: Better Auth provides first-party MFA: a twoFactor() TOTP plugin (totpURI QR, default 30s period, ±1 time-step tolerance), auto-generated single-use backup/recovery codes (regenerable via generateBackupCodes(); regeneration invalidates the old set), and passkeys (WebAuthn/FIDO2) via a SimpleWebAuthn-backed plugin. [dimension c]
findings.evidence: Source-level verification: the twoFactor plugin generates/validates TOTP, builds an otpauth:// totpURI, and uses @better-auth/utils verifyTOTP with default window=1 (i=-1,0,+1) and defaultPeriod=30; docs state verbatim it accepts codes 'from one period before and one after.' Backup codes are generated/stored on enable, single-use (removed after use), and regeneration deletes the old set. The passkey plugin docs state it is 'powered by SimpleWebAuthn behind the scenes,' corroborated by a real transitive-dependency build conflict (@simplewebauthn/server@13.2.1) and a dedicated Passkey/WebAuthn module. Note: avoid session.cookieCache pre-1.4.9 due to a 2FA-bypass advisory (see security finding).

findings.claim: Auth.js's WebAuthn/Passkeys provider is officially experimental and 'not recommended for production use,' and ships only on the still-beta next-auth v5 (>=5.0.0-beta.8, behind an experimental enableWebAuthn flag) — there is no stable-line passkey support. [dimension c/f]
findings.evidence: authjs.dev/getting-started/authentication/webauthn states verbatim 'The WebAuthn / Passkeys provider is experimental and not recommended for production use' and requires next-auth 5.0.0-beta.8+; a later docs page (beta.17) still shows the warning and still requires experimental:{enableWebAuthn:true}. npm dist-tags as of July 2026 show latest=4.24.14 (stable line is v4) and beta=5.0.0-beta.31 with NO stable 5.0.0, proving passkeys ship only on the beta v5 line. A claim that v5 hit stable in 2024 was a hallucinated search summary refuted by npm data. (No first-party TOTP/recovery-code system for Auth.js was surfaced in the verified claims — an inferred gap, not positively verified.)

findings.claim: Better Auth has built-in anti-user-enumeration on sign-up (returns an identical 200 whether or not the email exists when requireEmailVerification is on or autoSignIn:false, with timing mitigation, in v1.5+), but does NOT revoke a user's other active sessions on password reset unless revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset:true is set. [dimension d]
findings.evidence: email-password and security docs state verbatim that under those conditions sign-up 'prevents email enumeration by returning the same 200 response.' Code-backed: security issue #7972 (leaked existence via 422) fixed by merged PR #8091 for v1.5 (Feb 2026), returning 200 + simulated password hashing. Separately, docs state 'By default, other active sessions are not revoked when a user resets their password. To revoke all user sessions on password reset, set revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset to true' (corroborated by discussion #5526). Caveats: default config still returns 422 (anti-enum is opt-in via those settings and only in v1.5+); the synthetic 200 body can be distinguishable when plugins add user fields unless customSyntheticUser is configured (open issue #8096), so 'identical' is slightly strong. For this stack, enable both requireEmailVerification and revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset.

findings.claim: For the installed-PWA requirement, a hard web-platform constraint applies: a service worker (or any script) cannot read an httpOnly session cookie, because the Cookie Store / Async Cookies API deliberately excludes HttpOnly cookies; the commonly-proposed 'two-cookie split' mitigation was explicitly NOT supported by the cited spec discussion. [dimension e]
findings.evidence: whatwg/cookiestore issue #37 was closed by the spec editor with 'Exposing HttpOnly cookies to script would be a new capability' beyond the document.cookie-equivalent model; the current living explainer confirms 'Neither the query nor the monitoring API will include HttpOnly cookies.' MDN and Chrome docs agree. Practical consequence: a PWA service worker cannot read the httpOnly session cookie to check auth state, so auth-state visibility, offline gating, and Web-Push-to-session binding must be designed around server endpoints. The related recommendation to use a two-cookie split (httpOnly secret + non-httpOnly logged-in signal) was put to a vote and REFUTED (0-3) as not supported by the cited source — treat PWA/offline/Web-Push design as unresolved (see open questions).

findings.claim: Auth.js/NextAuth is now maintained by the Better Auth team and is in security-only maintenance mode; its own maintainers recommend Better Auth for new projects, and v5 remains beta with no immediate plan to ship a stable release. [dimension f]
findings.evidence: GitHub discussion #13252 (posted by lead maintainer balazsorban44, 2025-09-26, titled 'Auth.js is now part of Better Auth') states 'Auth.js...will now be maintained by the Better Auth team,' 'maintenance will continue for security and urgent issues,' 'If you're starting something new...we recommend Better Auth as the best way forward for most teams,' and 'We don't have any immediate plans for v5. But we'll keep maintaining both versions.' Independently confirmed by Better Auth's blog, the official authjs.dev 'migrate to Better Auth' guide, npm data (no stable 5.0.0; latest stable is v4.24.14), and discussion #13382 (2026) confirming v5 is still beta. This directly favors Better Auth for a greenfield 2026 build.

findings.claim: Lucia is deprecated/EOL: v3 was officially deprecated by March 2025 and repositioned as a documentation/learning resource for building session auth from scratch (npm package flagged deprecated) — it is no longer a library dependency to adopt. [dimension f]
findings.evidence: GitHub discussion #1714 ('A fresh start'), by maintainer pilcrowonpaper, opens 'It's official - I'll be deprecating Lucia v3 by March 2025' and 'Lucia is now a learning resource on implementing auth from scratch. You'll essentially recreate Lucia v3 in your project.' The official README adds a 'Why not a library?' section; npm view lucia deprecated returns a deprecation notice (latest v3.2.2, 2025-06-06); adapters were deprecated end of 2024 and bug fixes ended March 2025. Corroborated by multiple third parties. Lucia is disqualified as a primary auth dependency for this stack.

findings.claim: Better Auth carries a genuine security-maturity caveat: 31 GitHub advisories (3 critical/19 high/6 medium/3 low) spanning Dec 2024–Jun 2026 with 21 in 2026, including a critical premature-session-cookie-cache 2FA bypass (GHSA-xg6x-h9c9-2m83, fixed 1.4.9) and a high-severity org-invitation acceptance via unverified email match (CVE-2026-53514 / GHSA-fmh4-wcc4-5jm3, fixed 1.6.11, follow-up 1.6.14) — both hitting features this stack depends on. [dimension f]
findings.evidence: Verified exactly against the GitHub security-advisories API: 31 advisories, the stated severity breakdown, 21 in 2026 (15 in May, 4 in June), concentrated in newer enterprise plugins (SSO/SCIM/oauth-provider/Stripe). GHSA-xg6x-h9c9-2m83 (official severity CRITICAL, CVSS 9.1; claim's 'high' is a conservative understatement) confirms that with session.cookieCache enabled the sign-in session could be cached as valid before 2FA completed — implicating both the 2FA guarantee and the cookie-cache session model. GHSA-fmh4-wcc4-5jm3/CVE-2026-53514 (High, CVSS 7.7, fixed 1.6.11) let a user with an unverified session for the invited email accept an org invitation. Balancing note: the 2026 clusters are coordinated same-day disclosures from a dedicated security-review workstream (batch audits can be a maturity positive), so the 'immaturity' reading is one-sided — but the mitigation is concrete: pin to current patched versions and monitor advisories.

findings.claim: Concrete recommendation for this stack: adopt Better Auth with database-backed (revocable) sessions and TOTP + single-use recovery codes as baseline MFA, adding passkeys (WebAuthn) as step-up/passwordless; fallback is Auth.js v5 with a Postgres adapter if Better Auth's security cadence is unacceptable — accepting no built-in orgs/RBAC and experimental passkeys. [recommendation]
findings.evidence: Better Auth uniquely satisfies (a) built-in orgs/teams/RBAC + invitations, (b) DB-backed revocable sessions with log-out-all-devices, (c) TOTP + recovery codes + passkeys, and (d) anti-enumeration — while Lucia is EOL and Auth.js is maintenance-only with its maintainers explicitly recommending Better Auth. Choose database-backed sessions (not stateless) because multi-tenant B2B needs true revocation and because a PWA service worker can't read httpOnly cookies, making server-held session state the reliable source of truth. Operational guardrails driven by the advisories: pin to a current patched release (>=1.6.11/1.6.14 for the org-invite fix, >=1.5 for anti-enum, >=1.4.9 and avoid session.cookieCache for the 2FA-bypass class), enable requireEmailVerification and revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset. Marked medium because the composite recommendation is a judgment (the security-maturity caveat is real) even though every underlying fact is a high-confidence primary-source claim; the fallback (Auth.js v5 + adapter for revocable DB sessions) is viable but weaker given maintenance-mode status and missing first-party orgs/RBAC.

result.caveats: Time-sensitivity: all facts are as of mid-2026 and several are version-specific and will drift — re-verify current versions and the live advisory feed before committing (anti-enumeration requires v1.5+ and is opt-in; the 2FA-bypass is fixed in 1.4.9; the org-invitation flaw is fixed in 1.6.11 with follow-up 1.6.14; stateless sessions arrived in 1.4). Security-maturity signal is double-edged: Better Auth's elevated 2026 advisory count is real, but the clusters are coordinated same-day disclosures from a dedicated security-review workstream, so batch audits can be read as a maturity positive rather than pure immaturity — treat it as a reason to version-pin and monitor, not a disqualifier. Anti-enumeration is not on by default and its synthetic 200 body can still be distinguishable when plugins add user fields unless customSyntheticUser is set (open issue #8096), so 'identical' is slightly strong. Dimension (e) is only partially answered: the sole verified fact is that service workers cannot read httpOnly cookies; the popular 'two-cookie split' mitigation was explicitly REFUTED (0-3, not supported by the cited spec thread), and no verified claim covers offline auth UX or binding a Web Push subscription to a session/device — treat PWA/Web-Push design as an unresolved spike. A few comparative points about Auth.js/Lucia (e.g., 'no first-party TOTP,' 'no built-in orgs/RBAC') are inferred from absence in the verified claim set rather than positively verified. The final recommendation is a synthesis/judgment (medium confidence); its underlying facts are individually high-confidence, unanimous, primary-sourced claims. Source quality overall is strong (official docs, GitHub source-of-truth, GitHub Advisory Database, npm registry, WHATWG spec repo, maintainer announcements); the weakest inputs are third-party roundups used only as corroboration, and Better Auth's own docs/blog for the recommendation angle should be read with mild vendor bias in mind (though the Auth.js maintainers' independent endorsement offsets this).
openQuestions: Installed-PWA Web Push binding: how should a Web Push subscription be tied to a specific authenticated session/device, and how is the push subscription revoked when that session is revoked (log-out-all-devices)? No verified claim covers this, and it is central to the stack's requirement (e).

Offline auth UX: since a service worker cannot read the httpOnly session cookie and the 'two-cookie split' was refuted, what server endpoint or non-sensitive signal should gate offline/installed-PWA UI and re-validate on reconnect? Needs a design spike.

Does Better Auth's stateless (no-DB) session mode expose any revocation primitive (e.g., session versioning) strong enough for B2B 'log out all devices,' or is database-backed strictly required? Docs hint only at version + redeploy, which is likely inadequate for per-user revocation.

If the Auth.js v5 fallback is chosen, does it offer ANY first-party TOTP/MFA and multi-tenant organizations/RBAC, or must both be fully custom-built (increasing scope and security surface)? This gap was inferred, not positively verified, and materially affects the fallback's cost.

refuted.claim: The recommended architecture for making auth state visible to JS/ServiceWorker without weakening session security is a two-cookie split: an httpOnly cookie holding the session secret that JS/SW must never access, plus a separate non-httpOnly cookie that merely signals logged-in status (e.g. username or user id).
